review.translation: [Then he said|0], “[What|1] [have you done|2]? [The voice of|3] [your brother’s|5] [blood|4] [is crying out|6] [to me|7] [from|8] [the ground|9]!

analysis.evidence: וַיֹּאמֶר introduces the speaker’s question מֶה עָשִׂיתָ, “What have you done?”
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: In מֶה עָשִׂיתָ, “What have you done?”, מֶה is the direct object of עָשִׂיתָ. The question asks what deed Cain has committed, and the reference to his brother’s blood gives it accusatory force.
analysis.morphology: מֶה is an uninflected form of the interrogative מָה. It functions as a pronoun and has no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: מֶה עָשִׂיתָ means “What have you done?” The next clause says that Cain’s brother’s blood cries out from the ground, identifying the act as the killing of his brother.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, second person masculine singular. The ending ־תָ marks the subject.

analysis.evidence: קוֹל דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ means “the voice of your brother’s blood.” The plural participle צֹעֲקִים agrees with דְּמֵי, and אֵלַי gives the cry a hearer. The blood is personified as raising its voice to God.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine singular construct, without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Clarify how the plural construct and its agreeing participle identify Abel’s shed blood in the existing bloodshed sense.
draft.definition: Blood shed in a killing, here personified as a witness against the killer.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 4:10, דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ identifies the blood as the brother’s, and צֹעֲקִים describes it crying out from the ground.

analysis.evidence: דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ means “your brother’s blood.” The masculine plural participle צֹעֲקִים agrees with דְּמֵי. Abel’s shed blood cries out from the ground as a witness against Cain.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural construct noun, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: bloodshed and responsibility for a death

analysis.evidence: In דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ, “your brother’s blood,” the suffix addresses Cain and the noun identifies Abel as his brother.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix ךָ.

analysis.evidence: The plural צֹעֲקִים agrees with דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ, “your brother’s blood.” The blood is personified as crying from the ground. אֵלַי, “to me,” directs its appeal to God for justice over the killing.
analysis.morphology: Qal active participle, masculine plural, absolute

draft.change: Add Genesis 4:10 as evidence for the existing personal-recipient sense of אֶל in elah.
draft.definition: With a verb of speech or crying out, אֶל marks the addressee.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 4:10, צֹעֲקִים אֵלַי identifies the speaker as the hearer of the cry.

analysis.evidence: In צֹעֲקִים אֵלַי, “cry out to me,” the suffix identifies Yahweh, the speaker, as the one to whom the brother’s blood cries. מִן הָאֲדָמָה, “from the ground,” gives the source of the cry.
analysis.morphology: Preposition with a first-person common singular pronominal suffix.
analysis.sense: Marks the person to whom a cry is directed.

analysis.evidence: In צֹעֲקִים אֵלַי מִן הָאֲדָמָה, “crying out to me from the ground,” מִן marks the ground as the place from which the cry rises.
analysis.morphology: Independent Hebrew preposition with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In מִן הָאֲדָמָה, “from the ground,” מִן marks the ground as the place from which the blood of Cain’s brother cries out.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the absolute state with the prefixed definite article הָ.
analysis.sense: the ground underfoot; the face of the earth
